conversations.segment_role: Establishing the placement score and course details, then correcting the score from 74 to 72.

dialogue.content: Hey, I wanted to talk about this Portuguese writing course I just signed up for. It's through a platform called WriteInPT. I enrolled on May 8th and it's an eight-week program. The instructor is Professor Cláudia Mendes. I specifically chose a course focused on Brazilian Portuguese because I have zero interest in European Portuguese grammar drills — way too rigid for me.

That sounds like a great find! An eight-week Brazilian Portuguese writing course through WriteInPT with Professor Cláudia Mendes — that's a solid commitment. I can see why you'd want something that matches the way Brazilian Portuguese actually flows in everyday conversation rather than getting bogged down in formal European Portuguese conventions. Since you enrolled on May 8th, the course should wrap up around early July if it runs consecutively. How are you feeling about the course so far? Have you had any initial assessments or placement work to do?

Yeah actually, before the course started I took the vocabulary placement test for the WriteInPT course and scored 74 out of 100. It wasn't bad but honestly I was a little disappointed. I used to be really sharp with Portuguese vocabulary when I was younger. I grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese at home in São Paulo until I was about eleven, so it was deeply ingrained. But living in the US for so long, things slip.

A 74 out of 100 on a vocabulary placement test is actually a respectable score, especially considering you've been primarily in an English-speaking environment for a long time. The fact that you grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese at home in São Paulo until you were about eleven means you have a strong foundational base — that kind of early immersion really sticks even when active usage decreases. The course should help you reactivate a lot of that dormant vocabulary. Professor Cláudia Mendes probably structures the curriculum to build on existing knowledge rather than starting from scratch. Do you know what the course covers in the first few weeks?

The first couple of weeks are focused on narrative writing — short personal essays. That's actually what drew me to the course. I've been listening to a lot of MPB lately, Caetano Veloso and Maria Bethânia mostly, and the way Portuguese lyrics sit in melodies makes me want to write more expressively in the language. English songs just don't hit me the same way. There's something about the nasal vowels that hums.

Starting with narrative personal essays is a perfect way to reconnect with the language on an emotional level, especially given your connection to MPB. Caetano Veloso and Maria Bethânia are incredible choices — their lyrics have this poetic density that really showcases how Brazilian Portuguese can bend and flow. The way nasal vowels resonate in those melodies creates a texture that's hard to replicate in English. Using that musical inspiration as fuel for your writing assignments could produce some really beautiful work. You might even try writing about your relationship with Portuguese itself as one of those personal essays — the journey from São Paulo to now.

Oh wait, I need to correct something. I went back and checked the email confirmation from WriteInPT and my actual score was 72, not 74. I must have been misremembering. So 72 out of 100 is the real number. A bit lower than I thought, which is a little annoying, but it doesn't change my placement level or anything.

Thanks for double-checking that — so your confirmed vocabulary placement score is 72 out of 100 per the email from WriteInPT. That's still a solid score and as you said it doesn't affect your placement level. A two-point difference is minor in the grand scheme of things, and honestly, the score is just a snapshot of where you are right now. Given that you have deep roots in Brazilian Portuguese from childhood and you're actively re-engaging through MPB and this writing course, I'd expect that number to climb noticeably over the eight weeks. Shall I keep track of your course progress as you go through the weeks?

conversations.segment_role: Introducing the grandmother calls control target and updating the placement score to 68 after a grading recalculation.

dialogue.content: Sure, that would be helpful. Oh, and another thing — I started doing weekly Sunday calls with my grandmother in São Paulo back in late February, right after Carnaval. She was telling me about the blocos in her neighborhood during that first call. She doesn't speak any English at all, so the entire conversation is always in Portuguese. We talk every Sunday around 2 PM her time.

That's wonderful — weekly Sunday calls with your grandmother in São Paulo, started in late February right after Carnaval, at 2 PM her time. Since the conversations are entirely in Portuguese, those calls are also fantastic ongoing practice for your language skills. Hearing her talk about things like the blocos in her neighborhood must be a really grounding experience, keeping you connected to the culture and the everyday rhythm of Brazilian Portuguese. Between these calls, the MPB listening, and the WriteInPT course, you've built a pretty rich Portuguese immersion ecosystem for yourself. How long do the calls usually last?

Usually about forty-five minutes to an hour. She loves to talk. Honestly there's something about hearing her voice in Portuguese that just feels warm, like being wrapped in something familiar. It's the best part of my week. But anyway, I wanted to mention something about the course — I've been trying to read more in Portuguese too. I picked up 'Torto Arado' by Itamar Vieira Junior.

Forty-five minutes to an hour of pure Portuguese conversation every week is genuinely valuable immersion time, and the emotional warmth you describe makes it even more meaningful. That kind of affective connection to the language really helps with retention and fluency. As for 'Torto Arado' — that's a fantastic choice. Itamar Vieira Junior's prose is beautiful but also quite literary, so it's a real workout for reading comprehension. It won the Prêmio LeYa and has been widely celebrated. How far have you gotten? Are you finding it accessible or is it challenging after being away from Portuguese reading for a while?

Professor Cláudia Mendes emailed me today saying they recalculated scores because of a grading error on the idiomatic expressions section, and my corrected score is now 68 out of 100. That's lower than the 72 I thought I had. Kind of frustrating honestly. The idiomatic section was the part I felt most confident about, so hearing there was a grading error that brought my score down stings a bit.

That is frustrating — going from 72 down to 68 because of a recalculation on the idiomatic expressions section, especially when that was the part you felt strongest on. It's understandable that it stings. But keep in mind this was a grading error on their end, not a reflection of a sudden drop in your abilities. Professor Cláudia Mendes correcting it shows the program takes accuracy seriously. A 68 still puts you in a solid position, and your real-world Portuguese practice — the grandmother calls, the reading, the MPB immersion — matters far more than a placement number. Does the new score change your course track at all?

No, it doesn't change my track thankfully. I'm still in the intermediate-advanced group. I also got about 60 pages into Torto Arado and realized my reading speed in Portuguese has dropped a lot compared to when I was a teenager. I used to tear through books. It was discouraging — I felt kind of defeated for a couple days, like I'd let something slip away without noticing it happening.

Thanks, I appreciate that. My cousin Renata — she lives in Lisbon now — she told me back in April that she's been struggling with the European Portuguese pronunciation differences even though she grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese like me. She said the vowel sounds are way bigger differences than she expected. I found that kind of funny and also validating, like it's not just me who finds the European style stiff.

I'm sorry to hear about that feeling of defeat — it's a very real kind of grief when you notice a skill you once had so naturally has faded. Getting through 60 pages of a literary novel like 'Torto Arado' is still meaningful progress though, even if the pace feels slower than it used to be. The fact that you're still in the intermediate-advanced track despite the score adjustment to 68 confirms that your foundation is strong. Reading speed is one of those things that comes back with consistent practice. Between the WriteInPT course, your grandmother calls, and reading, you're actively rebuilding those neural pathways. Give yourself credit for showing up to the work.

That's a great example of how Brazilian and European Portuguese really are quite different in practice, not just on paper. If your cousin Renata grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese and is still struggling with European Portuguese vowel sounds after moving to Lisbon, that tells you the gap is real and substantial. The pronunciation differences — especially how European Portuguese tends to swallow vowels while Brazilian Portuguese keeps them open and melodic — can make it feel almost like a different language at times. It's completely validating for your preference for Brazilian Portuguese's natural flow. Renata's experience in Lisbon is a good reminder that your instinct to focus on Brazilian Portuguese in the WriteInPT course was the right call.

conversations.segment_role: Introducing the tentative score reversion and adversarial look-alike value; the confirmed score remains 68.

dialogue.content: So I had my second WriteInPT class this week and it went well. Professor Cláudia had us do a free-writing exercise about a childhood memory, and I wrote about Carnaval in São Paulo when I was eight or nine. It flowed really naturally once I got going. The other students seemed impressed that I could write so fluidly about sensory details — the sounds of the drums, the colors, the smell of street food.

That sounds like a wonderful exercise, and writing about Carnaval in São Paulo from childhood is such rich material. The sensory details you describe — drums, colors, street food smells — are exactly the kind of vivid, embodied writing that makes personal narrative powerful. The fact that it flowed naturally once you started is a really encouraging sign. It suggests your expressive capacity in Portuguese is stronger than that placement score might indicate. Your classmates' reactions make sense too — someone who grew up immersed in Brazilian culture and language brings an authenticity to that kind of writing that's hard to manufacture. Did Professor Cláudia give you any specific feedback on the piece?

She said my descriptive vocabulary was strong but I need to work on verb conjugation consistency — I apparently slipped between present and past tense a few times without realizing. That's fair criticism. She also mentioned that one student in the class scored 74 on the same placement test and had similar tense-switching issues, so it's apparently a common pattern for heritage speakers.

That's really useful feedback from Professor Cláudia. Tense-switching between present and past is incredibly common among heritage speakers — when you're writing from vivid memory, the brain naturally shifts into present tense because the sensory recall feels immediate, then snaps back to past tense for the narrative frame. It's actually a sign of emotional engagement with the material, not just carelessness. Interesting that another student who scored 74 on the placement test has the same pattern. It suggests this is a structural challenge for people who grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese but have been living in English-dominant environments. The verb conjugation work will probably be one of the most valuable parts of the eight-week course for you.

Professor Cláudia said there might be another adjustment because some students appealed, and if the appeal goes through my score would go back up to 72. She said they're reviewing it this week. I'm not holding my breath though — I'd rather just focus on improving through the actual coursework than obsess over a number.

That's a really healthy perspective. Whether the appeal brings your score back up to 72 or it stays at 68, the number is just a starting benchmark. What matters more is the trajectory you're on — the weekly writing exercises, the grandmother calls, the reading, the MPB immersion. All of that is doing more for your Portuguese than any single test score reflects. If the appeal does go through, great, but your attitude of focusing on the actual learning rather than the metric is exactly right. Professor Cláudia probably appreciates students who care more about growth than grades. Have you thought about what you want to write about for the next assignment?

I'm thinking about writing about my grandmother and those Sunday calls. There's something poetic about the way she speaks — she uses all these old expressions from interior São Paulo that I don't hear anywhere else. I want to try to capture that voice on the page. Also, my mom mentioned last week she's been mixing up Portuguese and English more than usual — she called a garfo a fork mid-sentence while talking to my aunt and didn't even notice. She's been in the US over twenty years so I guess that's expected.

That's a great idea actually — the generational language shift angle. My grandmother holding onto the old Portuguese, my mom blending languages, and me trying to reclaim something in between through this course. The eight-week course runs from May 8th so it should wrap up around early July. I want to have something meaningful to show for it by then, not just a score improvement but actual pieces of writing I'm proud of.

Writing about your grandmother and her unique way of speaking sounds like it could be a really powerful piece — capturing those old interior São Paulo expressions before they fade from living memory is almost an act of preservation. That kind of linguistic specificity is exactly what makes personal narrative writing come alive. As for your mom's code-switching, calling a garfo a fork without noticing is such a classic example of how bilingual brains start blending after decades of immersion in a second language environment. Twenty-plus years in the US would make that almost inevitable. It's actually a fascinating contrast — your grandmother preserving old regional Portuguese expressions while your mom is unconsciously merging Portuguese and English. You could even weave that generational language shift into your essay.

That three-generation framework — your grandmother as the linguistic anchor, your mom as the bridge where languages blur, and you as the one actively working to reclaim and reconnect — is genuinely compelling. It has real emotional and thematic depth. Since the course started May 8th and runs eight weeks, you're looking at wrapping up around early July, which gives you a nice arc to work with. Having tangible pieces of writing you're proud of is a much more meaningful goal than chasing a score. Between the Carnaval childhood piece and this grandmother essay, you're already building a small portfolio of personal narrative work in Brazilian Portuguese. Professor Cláudia Mendes seems like the right instructor to guide that process.
